Label read_highs_rules. I read the stock HiGHS 1.16 source (commit 283bfc859, unpatched copy) for every cheap rule our Stage 1 lacks, the postsolve stack entries and their undo code, the activity-sum helper, and mapped each rule to the switches and counters of HIGHS_DIAG.md and highs_diag.patch. I did not read PaPILO (not part of this label) and ran no remote command. The directory gpu_presolve/results/bench240/cheap_ablation did not exist while I worked, so no ablation file was used; I summed the DIAG counters of highs_cheap_all/summary.json and highs_stage1c/summary.json instead (script and output in /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-acoerduek--claude-spares-spare-bsnTJo/c660eb6b-7edc-4afc-bf62-0442cb32d870/scratchpad/stage1c_design/read_highs_rules/: agg_counters.py, counters_cheap_all.txt, counters_stage1c.txt, notes.txt).

Main findings. (1) All the single-column rules sit in two functions, colPresolve and singletonCol, in a fixed order: dominated / weakly dominated / forcing column first, then implied-integer conversion, dual fixing, stuffing, and for singletons free substitution and zero-cost singleton last. (2) The dominated-column tests are a test on the range of the reduced cost computed from bounds on the row duals. With only the original dual bounds (0 or infinite by row sense) the weak test is exactly the lock rule we already have; everything it adds comes from implied row-dual bounds, which HiGHS derives from non-integer columns whose bound side is strictly implied, keeps with a source column, and resets on every change that relaxes the premise. This dual-bound bookkeeping is the one new piece of state Stage 1c needs; implied equations, free substitution in inequality rows and the dominated tests all read it. (3) Rule bit 5 off also switches off bits 23 and 7 (forcing column is nested inside the weak test), which matters for reading the ablation runs. (4) In the cheap setting free column substitution (bit 8) only acts on singleton columns, so it has no fill-in; the fill-in and pivot limits belong to the aggregator. (5) Primal reductions (hold for every feasible point, with a recorded map): simple probing on equations, implied integer by the equation test, parallel-column merge (needs equal scaled costs), free singleton substitution in an equation, and as exact projections the zero-cost singleton and the forcing column (both need cost zero). Everything else (dominated, weakly dominated, dual fixing and its three extensions, stuffing, implied equations, free substitution in an inequality row, the weak implied-integer test, parallel-column dominance) keeps an optimal point only. (6) New postsolve needs: a column value computed from saved rows (forcing column, free singleton substitution, zero-cost singleton), an alias to a binary that has no doubleton row (simple probing, dual-fixing substitution), a merge record with a split procedure (parallel columns), a linear column transform (implied-integer scaling); all other rules leave fixed-column records or none. (7) Counters on the 240 instances with all cheap rules: weakly dominated 318,571 fixings, simple probing 296,239 substitutions, dual-fixing bound 205,092 fixings, parallel-column dominance 103,066, dual-fixing substitution 74,920, zero-cost singleton 58,511, dominated 47,210, parallel merges 24,233, implied integers 23,621, free substitutions 16,881, single-equation 13,017, implied equations 666, forcing columns 381, stuffing 73. Most are carried by one to four instances. (8) The 146 s that the cheap rules cost HiGHS on the 240 are mostly one instance: rd-rplusc-21 takes 105.8 s more, 80.8 s of it in the parallel-row loop; the parallel-column loop costs 2.3 s in total.

Tolerances in a MIP presolve (read): primal_feastol = mip_feasibility_tolerance = 1e-6 (HP:78-82, H/lp_data/HConst.h:387); dual_feasibility_tolerance = 1e-7 (HConst.h:383, H/lp_data/HighsOptions.h:847-848); small_matrix_value = 1e-9 (HighsOptions.h:818-822); kHighsTiny = 1e-14 (HConst.h:28). Bounds of non-continuous columns are rounded with feastol on every change (HP:1468-1472, 1496-1500).

Rule bits (read, HConst.h:291-314): 5 dominated column, 7 forcing column, 8 free column substitution, 13 parallel rows and columns, 17 dual fixing, 18 zero-cost singleton, 19 column stuffing, 23 weakly dominated column. Dependencies (read): if bit 5 is off, bit 23 is forced off (HP:532-533); the forcing-column code is inside the weakly-dominated lambda (HP:3701), which is only called when bit 23 is on (HP:3759). So 'bit 5 off' removes dominated, weakly dominated and forcing column together, 'bit 23 off' removes weakly dominated and forcing column, 'bit 7 off' only the forcing column. The value 9175456 of the Stage 1 reference is bits 5, 7, 8, 18, 19, 23 (computed); bit 17 stays on there and the switch dual_fixing_substitution cuts dualFixing down to the lock rule (G/baseline/highs_diag.patch:1766, G/baseline/HIGHS_DIAG.md:429-449).

Loop and order (read). Initial scan: rowPresolve on every row, then colPresolve on every column (HP:3864-3893). Fast loop: row singletons, changed rows, doubleton equations, singleton columns, changed columns, repeated while more than 0.01% of rows or columns went in the pass (HP:3895-3918; problemSizeReduction returns percent, HP:4321-4332). Main loop (HP:4077-4246): fast loop; aggregator; sparsify once; detectParallelRowsAndCols at most 5 times (HP:4139-4158), columns before rows; fast loop; the expensive stages. 'continue' to the top when a step removed more than 0.05%. HiGHS does not run the cheap rules to a fixed point.

Order inside colPresolve for a column with 2 or more entries (read, HP:3503-3634): (1) remove if fixed; (2) detectDominatedCol if bit 5 (HP:3536-3541); (3) MIP only: modifyImpliedRowDualBound for both bound sides (HP:3546-3578); (4) convertImpliedInteger (HP:3580-3583); (5) shift of a non-continuous column with range 1 to lower bound 0 by a linear transform (HP:3585-3603); (6) dualFixing if bit 17 (HP:3606-3615); (7) singletonColStuffing, which returns at once for a non-singleton (HP:3617-3627, H/presolve/HPresolveColStuffing.cpp:229-230); (8) updateRowDualImpliedBounds(col) only if the column is not of type integer (HP:3629-3631). Empty columns go to emptyCol, singleton columns to singletonCol (HP:3521-3534).

Order inside singletonCol (read, HP:2389-2494): row of size 1 -> singletonRow then emptyCol; detectDominatedCol without the immediate row-singleton cleanup (bit 5, HP:2409-2416); convertImpliedInteger(col,row) (HP:2418-2421); dualFixing (bit 17, HP:2423-2433); stuffing (bit 19, HP:2435-2444); updateColImpliedBounds for the one entry (HP:2446-2449); updateRowDualImpliedBounds for a non-integer column (HP:2452-2456); free column substitution if isDualImpliedFree(row) && isImpliedFree(col) and bit 8 (HP:2463-2485); zeroCostSingleton if bit 18 (HP:2488-2491).

Row-dual bounds, the state behind the dominated tests (read). Sign convention: reduced cost z_j = c_j - sum_i a_ij y_i. Original dual bounds rowDualLower/Upper are set by row sense: row_lower = -inf gives y <= 0, row_upper = +inf gives y >= 0, equations and ranged rows are free (HP:137-149). Implied bounds implRowDualLower/Upper start infinite and carry a source column (rowDualLowerSource/UpperSource, HP:139-143). impliedDualRowBounds keeps for every column two pairs of sums of a_ij*y_i with infinity counters: 'Orig' over the original dual bounds, and the plain one over the tighter of implied and original bound, where an implied bound is not used in the sum of its own source column (HP:1859-1863; H/util/HighsLinearSumBounds.h:21-36; H/util/HighsLinearSumBounds.cpp:152-174). Sums are HighsCDouble (double-double), updated incrementally.

Who derives implied row-dual bounds (read, HP:657-733). For a column j that is not of type integer (continuous or implied integer): its dual row gets the side sum a_ij y_i >= c_j when its lower bound is infinite or strictly implied (implColLower > col_lower + margin), and <= c_j when its upper bound is; margin is +feastol for columns with 2 or more entries and -feastol for singleton columns (HP:257-267, 669-673). A bound on y_r is derived only if the Orig dual sum of column j has at most one infinite term (HP:678-681); value = (c_j - Orig residual without row r)/a_rj (HP:697-698, 714-724); rejected if |value|*1e-14 > dual tol; stored only if it improves the current implied bound by more than 1000*dual tol = 1e-4 (HP:691, 704-711). So one derivation uses exactly one strictly implied column bound and otherwise only original dual bounds.

Second writer, MIP only (read, HP:3546-3578): if the lower (upper) bound of column j is implied in the non-strict sense (isLowerImplied, within feastol, HP:225-230) by its source row r, the Orig upper (lower) dual sum of j has exactly one infinite term, cost_j >= 0 (<= 0) and r is not ranged, then the implied dual bound of r is set to 0 on the side given by the sign of a_rj, with source j. This is allowed for non-integer columns, and for integer columns only when row r has integer columns only and all its coefficients are integral multiples of a_rj (HP:3555-3557). Inferred: the row's original dual bound already is 0 on that side, so the effect is to make the row 'dual implied free' (isDualImpliedGeq/Leq read the implied bound, HP:282-302), which makes it a legal pivot row for substituting an implied free column; changeImplRowDualLower/Upper then registers substitution opportunities (HP:1697-1698, 1722-1723).

Invalidation of implied row-dual bounds (read): on a coefficient change, all dual bounds sourced by the column are reset if its dual sums were relaxed, else only the one of that row; all are reset when the column is deleted (HP:926-941, 886-897). When a column bound is tightened or its implied bound relaxed so that the side is no longer strictly implied, the dual bounds derived from that side are reset (HP:899-924, called at HP:1479, 1507, 1614, 1662). When a row side becomes finite, the original dual bound is relaxed and the dual bounds sourced by every column of the row are reset (HP:971-978, 1000-1007). Row scaling divides them (HP:2091-2106). Re-triggering: a change of an original or implied dual bound marks all columns of the row as changed (HP:1556-1582, 1717-1721, 1764-1768); an implied dual bound turning strictly negative/positive marks the row as changed (HP:1688-1690, 1735-1737); an implied column bound that newly beats the explicit bound marks the column as changed (HP:1588-1593, 1636-1641).

Implied column bounds, for comparison with what our engine has (read, HP:735-828): derived from one row with the explicit bounds of its other columns (Orig residual) when at most one term of the row is infinite; stored with source row when better by more than 1000*feastol; in a MIP the explicit bound of a non-continuous column is tightened as well (HP:785-796, 801-812). The row counts as two-sided when it is an implied equation (HP:740-743). Reset when the source row is relaxed, changed or deleted (HP:873-884, 943-955, 986-988). The implied activity sums of a row use the tighter of implied and explicit bound, except in the source row (HighsLinearSumBounds.cpp:162-174).

Dominated column, bit 5 (read, HP:3636-3676, 3750-3757). Reduced-cost range from the implied dual sums: colDualLower = c_j - sup sum a_ij y_i, colDualUpper = c_j - inf sum a_ij y_i (HP:3645-3648; the plain sums, so several implied dual bounds from different source columns can enter one test). If colDualLower > dual tol: fix at the lower bound, or return dual infeasible (unbounded or infeasible) if the lower bound is infinite. If colDualUpper < -dual tol: fix at the upper bound. No integrality condition on the tested column. Change: fixColToLower/Upper (HP:4766-4798), then row singletons are removed at once except when called from singletonCol. Postsolve: FixedCol entry with value, cost and the column's entries (PSH:793-818); the primal undo sets x = value (PS:390-395). Cost: the sums are O(1); computeDynamism scans the column on every call (HP:3651). Counter: DIAG fixing dominated_col. Needs cost and row-dual argument; not a primal reduction.

Weakly dominated column, bit 23 (read, HP:3678-3700, 3759-3769). If colDualLower >= -dual tol and the lower bound is finite: fix at the lower bound; if colDualUpper <= +dual tol and the upper bound is finite: fix at the upper bound. Same record as above. Counter: DIAG fixing weakly_dominated_col. Not a primal reduction. Inferred from the code: with original dual bounds only, sup sum a_ij y_i is finite exactly when no row gives a down-lock and is then 0, so the weak test is 'no down-lock from rows and c_j >= -tol', which is the lock rule; everything the two tests add over the lock rule comes from implied row-dual bounds. Measured support: with all cheap rules on, dual_fixing_lock fixes 11 columns on the 240 instances and weakly_dominated_col 318,571 plus dominated_col 47,210; in the Stage 1 rule set dual_fixing_lock fixes 374,565 (G/results/bench240/highs_cheap_all/summary.json and highs_stage1c/summary.json, summed; HIGHS_DIAG.md:848-852 says the same for single instances).

Forcing column, bit 7 (read, HP:3701-3746). Reached only inside the weak test when the bound the column should go to is infinite. Second test on the Orig dual sum: |c_j - sup_orig sum a_ij y_i| <= max(dual tol / dynamism, machine eps), dynamism = max|a|/min|a| of the column. Inferred: this means the column has no row down-lock (direction to the infinite lower bound) and cost zero within that tolerance. Change: the column and every row it appears in are removed (HP:3729-3741). Postsolve: one ForcingColumn entry (cost, the other bound, column entries, flag infinite side, flag integral; PSH:890-902) pushed first, then one ForcingColumnRemovedRow per row with the row without the column and the side that binds (HP:3733-3739; PSH:905-916). Undo, in reverse: each row entry computes rhs - sum of the other columns (PS:316-327); the column entry takes, starting from the other bound, the minimum (maximum when the upper side is infinite) over rows of that residual / a_ij, rounded inward for an integral column with the MIP tolerance (PS:264-300). Cost: copies and removes all rows of the column. Counters: DIAG reductions forcing_column and forcing_column_removed_row. Needs the cost (zero) and a lock argument; as a map it is an exact projection (every reduced point extends, every original point projects, same objective).

Free column substitution, bit 8, as far as the cheap loop reaches it (read, HP:2457-2486; H/presolve/HPresolveAggregator.cpp:143-246). Only for a singleton column, so there is no fill-in and no size limit. Condition: column implied free = each bound infinite or implied within feastol (HP:221-248, 274-276); row dual implied free = equation, or finite upper side with implied dual upper <= dual tol, or finite lower side with implied dual lower >= -dual tol (HP:278-302). Inferred from HP:697-724 for a singleton: the implied dual bound of the row is c_j/a_rj, so an inequality row qualifies when the cost pushes the column against that side or is zero. An integer column must pass isImpliedIntegral (row has integer columns only, coefficients integral multiples of a_rj, and for an equation rhs/a_rj integral; in the inequality case the function rounds the row sides as a side effect, H/presolve/HPresolveImpliedInts.cpp:13-81). Change: row and column removed, cost c_j moved onto the other columns of the row with factor -c_j/a_rj and the offset adjusted, tiny costs (<= 1e-9) set to 0 (HPresolveAggregator.cpp:222-242). Postsolve: FreeColSubstitution with rhs (the equation side, or the upper side for a 'leq' row, the lower for 'geq'), cost, row type, the row and the column (PSH:577-594; HP:304-320); undo x_j = (rhs - sum of others)/a_rj (PS:85-99). Counter: DIAG reductions free_col_substitution. Equation pivot row: primal (exact, moves the cost). Inequality pivot row: needs the cost argument (the row is tight at an optimum).

Limits of the general substitution, which is the aggregator and not in the cheap set (read, HPresolveAggregator.cpp:14-132): row or column of length 2 always taken; pivot at least presolve_pivot_threshold = 0.01 of the maximum of the shorter line, else of the longer; fill-in = new entries minus (rowsize + colsize - 1) at most presolve_substitution_maxfillin = 10 (HighsOptions.h:1663-1665, 1710-1712); the loop stops after 3 fill-in rejections in a row; candidates sorted by length 2 first, then rowsize*colsize, then a hash.

Zero-cost singleton, bit 18 (read, H/presolve/HPresolveZeroCostSingleton.cpp:12-72). Condition: singleton column not of type integer (implied integer allowed), cost exactly 0, its row has both sides finite (equations included). Change: the column is deleted and the row sides become [L - max(a*lb, a*ub), U - min(a*lb, a*ub)], infinite where a column bound is infinite. Postsolve: ZeroObjSingletonContinuousCol with old and new row sides, column bounds, coefficient and the stored row (PSH:597-610); undo computes the row activity without the column and picks a bound of the column or the value that puts the row on a side, such that the original row holds (PS:1675-1762). Cost: one row copy. Counter: DIAG reductions zero_obj_singleton_col. No optimality argument: exact projection, needs cost zero. The one-sided case is left to dual fixing (comment at lines 15-19).

Column stuffing, bit 19 (read, HPresolveColStuffing.cpp:14-251). Start: a non-fixed singleton column whose row has 2 to 1000 entries and exactly one finite side (lines 229-239). For that side (as a <= row after sign flip): singleton columns of the row with a_j > 0, c_j >= 0 or a_j < 0, c_j <= 0 are counted at their dual-fixing bound; singletons with a_j > 0, c_j < 0 or a_j < 0, c_j > 0 are candidates, counted at the bound that minimises the row activity (lines 94-134). If all candidates are integer they must have equal |a_j|; if integer and continuous candidates are mixed, the integer ones are dropped (lines 139-170). Candidates sorted by c_j/a_j (lines 34-40, 190). In that order, with delta = |a_j|(u_j - l_j) and both bounds finite: fix at the cost-preferred bound if the Orig-style maximum activity plus delta still fits the side within feastol; else fix at the other bound if the minimum activity already exceeds the side by delta; both sums then grow by delta (lines 193-224). Record: FixedCol. Counter: DIAG fixing col_stuffing (73 columns on 3 of the 240 instances). Needs cost; not primal.

Dual fixing, bit 17: locks and the lock rule (read, H/presolve/HPresolveDualFixing.cpp:256-298; HP:3773-3799, 342-349). A row entry is a down-lock if (a < 0 and row upper finite) or (a > 0 and row lower finite), an up-lock in the mirrored case; a negative cost counts as a down-lock, a positive cost as an up-lock. No down-lock: fix at the lower bound if cost > dual tol or the lower bound is finite (an infinite lower bound with cost > tol returns dual infeasible through fixColToLower, HP:4769). No up-lock: mirrored. This is the part our engine has; it uses explicit row sides only, no redundancy test. Counter: DIAG fixing dual_fixing_lock. Difference read in our engine: E/src/rules_dual_fixing.cpp:40-55 compares the cost with exact 0 and leaves a zero-cost column with an infinite bound alone (HiGHS removes it as a forcing column).

Dual fixing, single-equation extension (read, HPresolveDualFixing.cpp:109-229, 300-315). Trigger: the column has locks both ways, exactly one down-lock or one up-lock, that lock is a row (not the cost) and an equation, and the row's flag singleEquationChecked is not set; the flag is set after the attempt and cleared when the row or any column of it is marked changed (HP:615-639). For every column k of the equation, with the sign taken so that its coefficient is positive: k is in S+ if its cost is >= 0 and in every other non-redundant row (isRedundant over implied sums, HP:331-340) the row is one-sided and the coefficient sign is such that decreasing k never hurts; S- is the mirror; any other ranged row disqualifies. If sup of the activity over all columns except the continuous ones of S+, plus inf over the continuous ones of S+, is <= rhs + feastol (all finite, explicit bounds), every column of S- is fixed at the bound that maximises its term; else, mirrored, every column of S+ is fixed at the bound that minimises its term. Record: FixedCol. Cost: for each column of the equation up to two scans of its column; no size limit, one attempt per row state. Counter: DIAG fixing dual_fixing_single_equation. Lock and cost argument; not primal.

Dual fixing, substitution (the part our switch dual_fixing_substitution names; read, HPresolveDualFixing.cpp:31-107, 316-331). MIP only. Trigger: locks both ways, a single down-lock or up-lock that is a row, both column bounds finite, and no unchecked single-lock equation in this call. Lock row must contain an integer column and have at most 1000 entries; if it has two finite sides, |a_col|(u-l) must be <= (U-L) + 2 feastol. For each non-fixed binary b of the row (type integer, bounds exactly 0 and 1): skip unless b = 0 makes the lock row redundant on explicit bounds (Orig residual sums); then compute the implied lower (upper) bound of the column from all rows that contain both columns with b = 1 (computeColBounds, HP:4334-4490, Orig residuals, rounded for a non-continuous column); if it reaches the upper (lower) bound within feastol, substitute col = l + (u-l) b for a single down-lock, col = u - (u-l) b for a single up-lock, first hit wins. Change: substitute() rewrites every row of the column and the cost (HP:4708-4764). Postsolve: DoubletonEquation entry with row = -1, coefficients 1 and -scale, rhs = offset (lines 97-100); undo x_col = offset + scale*x_b only (PS:146-151). Counter: DIAG substitutions dual_fixing. Lock and cost argument; not primal.

Dual fixing, bound strengthening (read, HPresolveDualFixing.cpp:231-254, 333-357; HP:4418-4456). For cost >= 0: worst-case lower bound = maximum over the down-lock rows of the value from which the row holds whatever the other columns do, i.e. (side - residual at the opposite extreme)/a with the implied (not Orig) residual sums; for a non-continuous column rounded up with tolerance feastol/max(1,|a|). If it is below upper - feastol and not huge (|.| <= feastol/1e-14 = 1e8): new upper = max(it, lower); if that equals the lower bound the column is fixed there (DIAG fixing dual_fixing_bound), otherwise the upper bound is changed only for non-continuous columns (DIAG bound_change dual_fixing), no postsolve entry. Mirrored for cost <= 0 and the lower bound, tried only if the first direction gave nothing. Runs for every column with locks both ways. Cost: one column scan with O(1) residuals and a vector allocation per call. Cost-sign and lock argument; cuts off feasible points; not primal.

Simple probing on an equation (read, HP:2688-2815). In rowPresolve, after redundancy, the binary row test, implied-equation conversion and the doubleton case. Condition: the row has an integer or implied-integer column, is an equation, minimum and maximum activity over implied bounds (getSumLower/getSumUpper) are finite and |min + max - 2 rhs| <= 1e-9; then the first column in column-index order (storeRow, HP:1821-1830) that is of type integer, has range 1 within feastol and |a| equal to max - rhs within 1e-9 is the binary. Every other column of the row: if already fixed it is removed as a fixed column (DIAG fixing simple_probing), else it is substituted by col = offset + scale*binary, with the two values taken from a snapshot of its implied-or-explicit bounds as this row sees them (HP:2728-2735, 2770-2808; same sign as the binary's coefficient: binary at upper gives the column's lower value). The row is then removed without its own postsolve entry (HP:2811). Postsolve: DoubletonEquation with row = -1 as above. Cost: O(1) test per equation visit, then one substitution per column of the row. Counter: DIAG substitutions simple_probing. Primal reduction: the alias holds for every feasible point.

Implied equation (read, HP:351-365, 2647-2664, 2523-2530). A row with a finite lower side whose implied dual lower bound is > +dual tol gets its upper side set equal to the lower side; mirrored for the upper side and an implied dual upper bound < -dual tol. A strictly signed dual with the matching side infinite returns dual infeasible. Postsolve: ImpliedEquation (row, side, row entries), used only by the dual postsolve (PS:429-438). The same two predicates are read without changing the row by the implied column bounds (HP:740-743), isImpliedIntegral and isImpliedInteger (HPresolveImpliedInts.cpp:28-34, 99-105). After the conversion the row runs through the equation rules of the same rowPresolve call (doubleton, simple probing, gcd). Counter: DIAG reductions implied_equation (666 on 11 of the 240 instances with all cheap rules). Row-dual (cost) argument; not primal.

Implied-integer conversion (read, HPresolveImpliedInts.cpp:83-184). Test for a continuous column: (a) equation test: some row of the column is an equation (or implied equation), has at most this one continuous column, rhs/a integral within feastol and all coefficients integral multiples of a within 1e-9; (b) only if no row was an equation and every row has no other continuous column: column bounds integral within 1e-9, and in every row all finite sides and all coefficients integral after division by a. Conversion sets the type to implied integer, increases rowsizeImplInt in its rows, and tightens the explicit bounds to the implied bounds with rounding (lines 159-183). Call sites in the cheap loop: colPresolve (HP:3580-3583), singletonCol (HP:2418-2421), after a parallel-column merge (H/presolve/HPresolveParallelRowsAndCols.cpp:446-453), and in rowPresolve for an equation with exactly one continuous column: if the integer coefficients and rhs have an integral scale <= 1000, the continuous column is scaled by x = s*z with s = 1/|a_c*scale| (postsolve LinearTransform, undo x = s*z + constant, PS:57-63), converted without the test, and the row scaled to integers (HP:2817-2858). The sweep detectImpliedIntegers runs only before probing (HP:4196). Counters: implied_integer_cols of DIAG total, DIAG bound_change implied_integer, part of linear_transform. (a) is a primal fact; (b) keeps an optimal point only (it removes feasible fractional values), although it reads no cost.

What a conversion changes for the other cheap rules (read): rows with an implied integer enter the integer block of rowPresolve (binary row test, HP:2568-2583; all-integer scaling and rounding count implied integers, HP:2971; coefficient strengthening skips only continuous columns, HP:3330); implied bounds are written to the explicit bounds (HP:787-788, 803-804); dual-fixing bound strengthening changes the bound (HPresolveDualFixing.cpp:342, 353); it counts as integer in the test of other continuous columns (HPresolveImpliedInts.cpp:93). It is still treated as non-integer by: implied row-dual bounds (HP:3630, 2452), the zero-cost singleton (HPresolveZeroCostSingleton.cpp:20), parallel columns (type-integer tests, HPresolveParallelRowsAndCols.cpp:190-232) and isImpliedIntegral, which requires true integers (HPresolveImpliedInts.cpp:22-23). A substituted true integer upgrades an implied-integer representative to integer (HP:4716-4725).

Parallel columns, detection (read, HPresolveParallelRowsAndCols.cpp:22-112). One pass over all nonzeros gives per column the entry of largest |a| (ties within 1e-9: smallest row index) and a hash over (row, a/that entry); a singleton column gets its row index as hash, so all singleton columns of one row fall into one bucket. Columns are visited in index order against an unordered_multimap of earlier columns; candidates of different length are skipped; the first candidate that leads to a reduction ends the scan for this column. constraints_for_design: Primal-only mode: of the Stage 1c rules only these hold for every feasible point and may stay on: simple probing on equations, implied integer by the equation test (with its column scaling), parallel-column merge, free singleton substitution with an equation as pivot row. Off, because they keep an optimal point only: dominated and weakly dominated column, dual fixing with all three extensions, stuffing, implied equations (and with them the two-sided reading of such rows in implied bounds and integrality tests), free substitution with an inequality pivot row, the weak implied-integer test, parallel-column dominance. Zero-cost singleton and forcing column are exact projections (crush = drop the column, same objective) but read the cost and, for the forcing column, the locks; the plan (DESIGN.md section 4 and 8) currently puts them in class D, so a decision is needed if they are to run in primal-only mode.

The dominated tests need new state that Stage 1 does not have: per row an implied dual lower and upper bound with source column, per column the range of sum a_ij y_i in two versions (original dual bounds; implied bounds with the column's own contributions excluded) with infinity counters, as compensated sums like the row activities. Every event HiGHS resets on must reset ours: coefficient change in the source column, source column deleted, the bound side of the source column no longer strictly implied (explicit bound tightened or implied bound lost), a row side turning finite, row scaling, row merge. The plan's guard 'row-dual bounds are never carried across a structural batch' is a simpler rule that covers these.

Build order follows from HiGHS's dependencies: without implied row-dual bounds the dominated and weakly dominated tests add nothing over the existing lock rule, implied equations never fire, and free singleton substitution is limited to equation rows. The forcing column, zero-cost singleton, stuffing, the dual-fixing extensions, simple probing, the equation test for implied integers and parallel columns do not need the dual state.

Postsolve records. Fixed-column records suffice for: dominated, weakly dominated, stuffing, lock rule, single-equation extension, bound strengthening (when it fixes), parallel-column dominance, columns already fixed in a simple-probing row. New kinds: (1) column value from saved rows: forcing column (all its rows, the binding side of each, the other bound, integrality for inward rounding), free singleton substitution (one row and the side to make tight), zero-cost singleton (one row, both original sides, column bounds; any value in the intersection is valid, so the choice must be fixed and deterministic); (2) an alias to a binary with no doubleton row behind it (simple probing, dual-fixing substitution): our alias_record_t has a row field described as the doubleton equation (E/include/gprs/postsolve.hpp:27-35), so either a row-less variant or a new kind is needed; (3) a merge record (scale, both bound pairs, both types) with a deterministic split; HiGHS's fallback search of up to 1000 unit steps should not be copied; (4) a linear column transform x = s*z + t for the implied-integer scaling. Per the lesson of Entry 25 each of these comes with its reader in the structure check and with mutants.

What the structure check can prove differs by rule. Primal rules can be checked from the record alone: a simple-probing alias against the equation and the bounds, a merge against the two original columns and the no-hole conditions, an equation-test implied integer against the row. Dual rules cannot be proved by a solver-free structural reading of a single record beyond their premises (lock counts, cost signs, the row being one-sided, redundancy of the lock row at b = 0, the implied bound at b = 1); their correctness has to come from the exact oracle on tiny MIPs and from the reduced-MIP optimum on real instances.

Saved-row invariant (DESIGN.md section 8): the forcing column removes rows whose other columns stay live, and its undo reads their final values; the free singleton and zero-cost singleton records also read other columns of the saved row. These rows must contain no column whose record is undone later, exactly as for the existing records. HiGHS relies on stack order for this.

Determinism: HiGHS's parallel-column pass depends on the iteration order of equal keys in an unordered_multimap and stops at the first reducing candidate, and simple probing takes the first matching binary in column-index order. Our engine needs a defined order for both (sorted groups; a stated tie-break for the binary and for which of two parallel columns survives).

Budgets the owner requires and HiGHS lacks: the implied-integer test (rows of the column times their length on every visit), the single-equation extension (sum of the column lengths of an equation), the dual-fixing substitution (binaries of the lock row times column lookups), bucket scans of parallel columns where many singleton columns share a row, and the substitution work of simple probing (one column rewrite per column of the row). HiGHS's own caps are only the two 1000-entry row limits and 5 calls of the parallel stage.

Tolerances to carry into the rule table (DESIGN.md section 6): dominated strict at dual tol, weak at -dual tol; implied dual bound recorded only if better by 1000*dual tol and not huge; 'strictly implied' margin +feastol, but -feastol for a singleton column; forcing column |cost| <= max(dual tol/dynamism, eps); simple probing midpoint and coefficient match at 1e-9; parallel entries at 1e-9, merge cost difference at dual tol; implied-integer integrality of sides at feastol and of coefficients at 1e-9, integral scale at most 1000; worst-case bound rounded with feastol/max(1,|a|) and rejected above 1e8. For primal-only mode the merge needs exactly equal scaled costs if 'equal objective' is to hold exactly.

Fixed point: HiGHS's cheap loop stops on a 0.01% threshold and never promises a fixed point; our engine does where it says so. Rules with a one-shot guard in HiGHS (singleEquationChecked, first-hit binary in the substitution, the else-branch order of bound strengthening) need a definition of 'nothing left to find' on our dirty lists, or must be declared outside the fixed-point claim.

Reading the ablation files when they arrive: bit 5 off also removes the weak test and the forcing column; with bits 5 and 23 off the lock rule takes most of what the weak test fixed (374,565 lock fixings in the Stage 1 rule-set run), so that ablation measures only what the implied dual bounds add; with bit 17 off the weak test takes the lock-rule columns, so that ablation measures the three extensions together.

Time gate: the extra HiGHS time of the cheap rules is not a cost of the column rules themselves; 105.8 of 145.6 s is one instance in the parallel-row loop (rd-rplusc-21). The time rule for Stage 1c should be read against HiGHS per instance, and our existing parallel-row rule should be run on rd-rplusc-21 after column rules create many singleton columns.
open_questions: HiGHS's dominated tests read the dual sums over all implied row-dual bounds at once (HP:3645-3648), so one conclusion can rest on several strictly implied column bounds, while each single implied dual bound is derived from one. The plan's guard says 'at most one implied premise per derivation'. Does the guard apply to the dominated test as a whole (then we find less than the reference), or only to each derived dual bound as in HiGHS? I did not establish whether HiGHS's combined use is always valid.

HiGHS fixes on weak domination (reduced-cost bound >= -dual tol) also when the bound comes from implied dual bounds, and derives implied dual bounds from implied-integer columns as well as continuous ones. The plan's guards say 'continuous columns only, strictly beyond the dual tolerance'. The lock-rule-equivalent part of the weak test is safe; how much of the 318,571 weak fixings needs implied dual bounds is not visible in the counters. The ablation files (bit 5, bit 23) are needed for this.

The MIP-only step that sets an implied dual bound to 0 for a non-strictly implied bound side, including for integer columns in all-integer rows with integral coefficient ratios (HP:3546-3578), only matters for pivot-row eligibility. With the aggregator out of Stage 1c, is it needed at all now, or only for free singleton substitution in inequality rows?

Simple probing uses the activity range over implied bounds, also those of continuous columns that our engine keeps apart from the explicit bounds. Should our test read the recorded implied bounds (as HiGHS does) or explicit bounds only? With explicit bounds only, instances whose equation is balanced only through implied bounds of continuous columns would be missed; I did not measure how many of the 296,239 substitutions these are.

Should the zero-cost singleton be allowed on an implied-integer column as in HiGHS (only type integer is excluded)? After the column is gone nothing enforces its integrality except the row that implied it; if integrality was derived by the weak test, the undo value may be fractional.

HiGHS's second stuffing condition (fix at the non-preferred bound only if the minimum activity already exceeds the side by the candidate's whole range, HPresolveColStuffing.cpp:208-219) is stricter than the rule in the paper it cites; the source comment gives a basis-postsolve reason that does not apply to a MIP. With 73 fixings on 3 of 240 instances: build the paper's rule, HiGHS's, or leave stuffing out of Stage 1c?

Dual-fixing bound strengthening changes bounds of integer columns without a postsolve entry and cuts off feasible points; the crush of a known feasible point then fails the bound. How should check/gprs_check treat such instances (crush check off for dual rules, as in primal-only reasoning, or a repair step)? The same holds for implied equations and the weak implied-integer test.

Forcing column for an integer column: the undo rounds the value inward from the tightest row. HiGHS has no condition that the rounded value still satisfies the rows; it does, since moving further in the free direction keeps every removed row satisfied (inferred from the lock condition), but the oracle should cover integer forcing columns with non-integral row residuals.

Whether PaPILO's versions of these rules (DualFix, DominatedCols, SingletonCols, SingletonStuffing, ParallelColDetection, SimpleProbing, ImplIntDetection) use different conditions was not read under this label; another reader has to supply that before conditions are fixed.

Main findings.
1. Rule mapping. PaPILO's FreeVarSubstitution works on equations of any length and is the counterpart of HiGHS's aggregator (a later stage), not of HiGHS rule 8, which in the cheap set fires only on singleton columns; PaPILO's counterpart of rule 8 is the equation case of SingletonCols. PaPILO's DualInfer is the counterpart of HiGHS's implied row-dual bounds, which feed dominated column, forcing column, implied equations and implied-free singletons in inequality rows; PaPILO has no weakly dominated column by a reduced-cost bound.
2. Where PaPILO is stronger than HiGHS: dual bound strengthening changes continuous columns too (HiGHS only non-continuous ones, or fixes); a singleton column of an equation is removed when only one bound is implied, also with a cost (the row stays as an inequality); DualInfer propagates dual bounds to a fixed point.
3. Where HiGHS is stronger: single-equation extension and binary substitution in dual fixing; zero-cost singleton in a ranged row; stuffing with one candidate, with equal-weight integer candidates and with fixing at the non-preferred bound; parallel columns with unequal cost (fix the worse one) and without the pure-binary exclusion; implied integers through implied equations; simple probing with any range-1 integer and no fill-in limit.
4. Safety. PaPILO compares with absolute 1e-9 on plain (uncompensated) activity sums and counts every bound of size 1e8 or more as infinite; HiGHS uses its feasibility tolerance (1e-6 in MIP) on compensated sums and divides the tolerance by the coefficient when it rounds a worst-case integer bound. Both refuse dual-strengthened bounds beyond 1e8. PaPILO's SingletonCols does not test the integrality of side/a before it removes an integer singleton (SingletonStuffing does); read, not run.
5. cuOpt's two reductions. The BHW core is a free function without PaPILO types but uses <bit>, _Float128, __int128 and GCC overflow builtins; it leaves no primal postsolve data. Single-lock dual aggregation is written entirely against PaPILO's problem views; its core is one row scan with two activity sums and emits x = y or x = 1 - y; it is a dual reduction and is narrower than HiGHS's dual-fixing substitution in the column type and wider in the polarity of the binary.

constraints_for_design: Scope by rule, so that Stage 1c does not take in a later stage by mistake: HiGHS rule 8 in the cheap set is the substitution of implied-free singleton columns only; substitution of longer columns is the aggregator (PaPILO's Substitution) and belongs to the next step of amendment A8. PaPILO's parallel columns only merge; fixing the worse of two parallel columns with unequal cost exists only in HiGHS's parallel-column code.

Dominated, weakly dominated and forcing columns, implied equations and implied-free singletons in inequality rows all read bounds on row duals. The engine needs that state (two bounds per row with a source column), derived from continuous columns only as DESIGN.md section 4 already demands. The references show two ways to keep it sound: HiGHS takes only strictly implied column bounds and one step per column with a minimum improvement of 1000 dual tolerances; PaPILO takes weakly implied bounds but removes each bound it uses from a private copy of the activities and propagates to a fixed point with a minimum relative improvement of 1e-3 and no cap on rounds. Whichever is chosen needs a work budget; PaPILO's loop has none.

Do not copy PaPILO's absolute 1e-9 tests on plain sums. Implied-bound, redundancy and 'min + max = 2 * side' tests should use the engine's compensated activities with their error bound (G/include/gprs/numerics.hpp:29-31, 121-126). A rule that moves a column to a worst-case bound (dual bound strengthening, stuffing, single-lock aggregation) puts points on the edge of a row, so an integer bound of that kind should be rounded with the tolerance divided by |a|, as HiGHS does (H/presolve/HPresolve.cpp:4442-4454).

Bounds and sides created by the new rules need a size guard: both references refuse a dual-strengthened bound of 1e8 or more, and PaPILO never uses a bound of that size in an activity. This applies to dual bound strengthening, to the sides side - a * bound of a removed slack, to the widened sides of a zero-cost singleton and to the bounds of a merged column; it has to agree with tol.infinite_term and tol.side_error.

New postsolve records, each with its reader in the structure check and its mutants: (1) column from a saved row, x = (side - sum of the others)/a, for implied-free singletons and removed slacks; for a removed slack the check has to show that the bounds of x follow from the sides of the row that stayed; (2) fixed at infinity or forcing column, with the saved rows, value chosen in postsolve as an extreme over the rows; (3) parallel-column merge with both bounds, both types and the scale; the check has to show that every value of the merged column can be split, which is the no-hole condition; (4) zero-cost singleton with the old sides, the column bounds and the coefficient. crush must be extended for (3), where the reduced value is col2 + scale * col1, not a copy.

The alias record names 'the doubleton equation row' (G/include/gprs/postsolve.hpp:27-35). Aliases from simple probing come from a longer equation plus bounds, and aliases from single-lock aggregation and from HiGHS's dual-fixing substitution come from a dual argument. The record needs an origin so that the structure check reads the right premise, and the dual kind must be off in primal-only mode.

Reductions without primal postsolve data still need to be visible to the checks: a dual-strengthened bound and an implied equation cut off feasible points, so the crush check of a known feasible point fails on them unless the engine reports them as dual reductions; implied-integer conversion by the inequality test is of the same kind. Implied integers by the equation test, simple probing, zero-cost singletons, removed slacks of equations and BHW keep every feasible point (up to the choice of the removed column's value) and can stay on in primal-only mode.

An integer column is removed through a row only when all other columns are integer, all ratios are integral and the scaled side is integral, with infeasible when it is not (DESIGN.md section 4 has this guard). PaPILO's SingletonCols omits the test of the side; the engine's oracle campaign should hold a case for it (2x + 2y = 3 with x a singleton integer).

Determinism: PaPILO breaks ties with random row and column permutations and sorts with pdqsort; HiGHS depends on hash-bucket order. The engine needs index tie-breaks everywhere; in stuffing the order by cost/coefficient should be compared by cross-multiplication with the index as the last key, so that the set of fixed columns is the same on every machine.

Batch validity: lock-based fixings found on one state are valid together. Implied-free substitutions, removed slacks, weakly dominated columns and the fixing of one of two parallel columns each rest on a bound implied by rows that another reduction of the same batch may change. PaPILO rejects such transactions by locks, HiGHS applies one at a time. In the host engine these rules must be applied one transaction at a time with the premise re-tested (DESIGN.md section 3 item 2), and the implied bound used must be the one-hop bound of a named row.

Budgets seen in the references: stuffing on rows of at most 1000 entries (HiGHS) and once per row rather than once per singleton; dual-fixing substitution on rows of at most 1000 entries; fill-in at most 10 per substitution (both); parallel columns need a cap on comparisons per bucket like options_t::parallel_bucket_limit, since neither reference has one; BHW costs 2^k points with k <= 12 plus a search over weight vectors per new shape and needs a unit count and its ordered cache; single-lock aggregation is one pass over the nonzeros for the locks and one scan per lock row.

Fixed point: PaPILO divides the row by |a| when it removes a slack; in the engine a rescaled row would meet gcd and coefficient tightening again, so the row should be left in its own units and the tolerance handled as in the constraint on worst-case bounds. BHW has to run after row tightening has settled and tightening has to run again after it; both only lower coefficient sizes, and BHW accepts a row only when its largest coefficient shrinks or an entry drops, so the alternation ends.

Port of BHW into the standalone engine: take bhw_reduce_row and the scaling helper, replace std::countr_zero, _Float128 (by the engine's compensated sums), __int128 (by a 64x64 to 128-bit product or a cap on the scaled coefficients that keeps products in 64 bits), the overflow builtins and cuopt_assert; write a new wrapper on the engine's row view next to the tightening family; no postsolve record, but the structure check needs a reader for 'same 0/1 feasible set, relaxation not weaker', which it can do by enumeration for k <= 12.

Port of single-lock aggregation: rewrite on the engine's state (locks, lock row, compensated row activities), keep the three tests (implication on the lock row beyond the feasibility tolerance, redundancy of the row with the partner at its other value on every finite side, coefficient ratio guard), give the redundancy test a margin from the activity error bound since cuOpt compares without one on plain sums, lock the bounds of all columns of the row as premises, and record an alias of dual origin. HiGHS's dual-fixing substitution covers the same case for non-binary columns and uses all shared rows; one engine rule can cover both.
open_questions: Should dual bound strengthening change bounds of continuous columns? PaPILO does, HiGHS only changes non-continuous columns or fixes. In the engine explicit bounds of continuous columns are not touched before make_explicit; a bound from a dual argument is neither a recorded implied bound nor an input bound, so where it lives has to be decided.

Removed slack with a cost when only one bound is implied (PaPILO only): the cost moves onto the other columns of the row and the row stays as an inequality. What column rules can build on. The state has a column store (CSC with the slot of each entry in the row store, live length per column in O(1)), cost and a compensated objective offset, up and down lock counts kept consistent by every state operation, column status (live, fixed, removed), row activities with the count and position of infinite terms, and, for continuous columns only, one recorded implied lower and upper bound with its source row and that row's version. There is one column work list for rules (dual fixing), fed by every change of a column's entries, locks or cost. Rule-level helpers exist to tighten a bound, fix a column at a finite value, delete or move an entry, change sides, delete a row, and to substitute one column by another through the alias forest (inside the doubleton family only).

What they have to add. (1) There is no dual information at all: no bounds on row duals, no reduced-cost bounds; the dual tolerance is defined and only hashed. (2) Column events are missing for everything except entries, locks and cost: a change of the column's own bound, of a finite side of one of its rows, of a neighbour's bound (row activity), or a row scaling puts no column on a list. (3) A row cannot gain an entry, so only substitutions without fill-in fit the present storage. (4) There is no operation to change a column type and no safe way to relax a bound (records taken from rows of that column are not voided). (5) The postsolve stack has four fixed-size record kinds (fixed column, alias, parallel row, row addition); there is no record for a column defined by a row, for a column fixed at infinity with its rows, or for merged columns, and crush is only a restriction to the kept columns. (6) Budgets are per call; nothing caps a family over the whole presolve.

Driver. A family is a class with run(state, budget, postsolve, options) called through engine_t::call, which makes the budget from options.budget[rule], books statistics and collects findings, stopped and limited. Its model class has continuous columns only as line columns, at most one per row, so several continuous columns in one row (stuffing over several continuous singletons, parallel or dominated continuous pairs) are outside it, and the generator has no knob for parallel columns. With the first dual rule beyond the lock rule these four have to change in the same commit, or they report false failures or stay silent: the oracle's primal condition (oracle.cpp:1005-1007), the default-mode argument and verdicts of the crush check (crush_check.hpp:20-38, gprs_check.cpp:394-399 and the cost variants 430-453), and the planted-point test (test_e2e_planted.cpp:267-291).

For a dual reduction (one that cuts feasible, non-optimal points) the oracle's comparison of outcome and optimal value is the only exact check. The structure check passes any fixing inside the original bounds and any alias with transferred bounds, right or wrong; the crush check cannot be applied in default mode; on real instances only HiGHS proving the reduced optimum or a reduced bound above a known value can show an error. So each dual rule must be exercisable inside the oracle class, and its mutants must be run through the campaign, not only through gprs_check.

What the oracle class must contain per rule (read from oracle.hpp and oracle.cpp; the rule names are the brief's): free and half-free continuous columns in several rows with and without cost (present: line columns, p_infinite_bound, p_zero_cost) for dominated, weakly dominated and forcing columns, implied equations and the dual-fixing extensions; a continuous singleton column in an equation or inequality with integer neighbours, with zero and nonzero cost (present only with p_singleton_col > 0 or --singletons) for free column substitution, zero-cost singleton and stuffing with one continuous singleton; a continuous column in an equation whose other columns are integer with integral ratios (present) for implied-integer conversion; binaries in equations (present, profile binary) for simple probing. Missing: parallel columns of any type (no knob); two or more continuous columns in one row, which stuffing over several continuous singletons, parallel continuous columns and dominated continuous pairs need and the class forbids.

Structure check per reduction, inferred from its code. Column defined by a row: column_map_t must become a combination of several reduced columns; the bounds test stays a box test only if the implied-free proof used the pivot row alone, a proof from another row needs the reduced image of that row as in kept_rows. Cost: nothing is checked today, so a test that the composed original cost equals the reduced cost plus offset should be added with the first rule that moves cost by a row. Merged columns: the check has to verify proportional entries in every original row, the cost ratio and the split domain, since the postsolved pair is not a function of one reduced column. Rows deleted with a column fixed at infinity: they do not hold over the reduced bounds, so the present rows test would fail; the check needs an existence test for the removed column.

Budget and limits. Each family needs its own entry in options_t::budget and must spend per entry read; a pairwise search (parallel columns) needs a bucket limit and must report limited when comparisons end on it, as the parallel rows do (rules.hpp:228-233); a cap that depends on what the presolve did earlier must return the list (stopped) or report limited, never skip silently. The owner's rule that no rule may dominate the time is met per call only; a total per presolve does not exist.

Determinism. The family contract of rules.hpp:78-82 applies: results from state, options and budget only, work data by index, new state arrays inside state_hash. The hashing and bucket code that parallel columns could reuse is private to rules_parallel_rows.cpp (lines 24-150 and 515-545).

A type conversion (implied integer) must clear the column's implied-bound records, because the consistency check forbids a record on an integer column (state_storage.cpp:857-859), must round its bounds as the start step does (presolve.cpp:77-92), and must list its rows for row tightening, which acts on rows whose free columns are all integer (rules.hpp:168-177).

An alias that does not come from a doubleton row (dual-fixing substitution, simple probing, single-lock dual aggregation) cannot go through the doubleton family as it is: an edge needs a row, the family deletes that row, and the alias record asserts a row index (rules_doubleton.cpp:214-216, postsolve.cpp:107-117). The apply functions have to be shared or a second entry added.

The design principle. Today only the oracle can tell whether a dual reduction is right (reader engine; E/check/crush_check.hpp:20-38 says its default-mode argument ends with the first new dual rule). I therefore admit a rule into Stage 1c only if it has a forward map: a crush step under which every feasible point of the model before the reduction becomes a feasible point of the model after it with an objective that is not higher, and an undo under which every feasible point of the reduced model comes back feasible with the same objective. The two together prove that the optimum is kept, and both can be tested on any known feasible point without a solver, on tiny oracle models, on planted models with several continuous columns per row, and on the 173 benchmark instances that have points. A rule whose only proof is LP duality has no such map and is not built.

Result. Nine rules are built, in two classes. Exact (every feasible point crushes with equal objective, on in primal-only mode): zero-cost singleton, free singleton column in an equation, forcing column, simple probing on equations, parallel-column merge. Exchange (dual, off in primal-only mode, each with a recorded crush step): parallel-column dominance, free singleton column in an inequality row, dual bound strengthening, dual substitution to a binary (this one also covers cuOpt's single-lock dual aggregation). Five rules of amendment A8 are not built in Stage 1c: dominated and weakly dominated columns by reduced-cost bounds, implied equations, the single-equation extension of dual fixing, column stuffing, implied-integer conversion. decisions_for_owner: Rule list. Amendment A8 names dominated and weakly dominated columns, implied equations, the dual-fixing extensions as a whole, column stuffing and implied-integer conversion for Stage 1c. I leave out the first two, the single-equation part of the third, and the last two. Reason: none has a forward map that the crush check can test, HiGHS's own ablation puts them at 1.0006 together, and without them the engine needs no row-dual state. If you want the dominated test anyway, the compensator form in its rule entry is the one I would build, after milestone 5. Recommended: accept the shorter list and look again at the gate.

Primal-only mode. The zero-cost singleton and the forcing column read the cost (it must be zero) and the forcing column reads locks, and DESIGN.md sections 4 and 8 put them with the dual rules. Both keep the contract of the mode as E/include/gprs/presolve.hpp:83-85 words it: every feasible point crushes to a feasible point with the same objective. I switch them on in primal-only mode, which lets the crush check test them at full strength, and relax the round-trip clause (z equals x) for the columns whose value the undo chooses. The alternative is to keep them off there and leave the clause as it is.

Merge of binaries. Two parallel binaries with equal cost become one integer column with range 2, as in HiGHS; PaPILO switches parallel columns off on pure binary models. I follow HiGHS because it is the reference. Say so if the later clique and probing stages should keep binaries; the merge would then be limited to pairs whose merged column is not a former binary pair.

Singleton column with a cost when only one of its bounds is implied (PaPILO removes it and keeps the row as an inequality). Not taken: HiGHS does not do it, it makes the objective denser, and its worth is in no measurement. It fits the saved_rows_col record without change if you want it measured.

Tolerances stricter than the reference: exact zero cost for rules 1 and 3, costs equal to 1e-12 relative for a merge, the forcing-row tolerance of the engine for simple probing instead of HiGHS's absolute 1e-9. I chose them so that the objective identity and the row tolerance of the checks hold without exceptions. They can be loosened one at a time after the gate shows what they cost.

Oracle class. I do not extend the exact oracle to rows with two continuous columns; those cases are covered by the planted-point test with the forward crush. The alternative is an oracle that merges parallel line columns before it solves, which adds an implementation of the merge to the checker itself.

A cap per column over the whole presolve (max_col_tests = 16 for rules 8 and 9), in addition to the per-call budgets, with the fixed-point flag cleared when it is hit. This is the only total cap in the design; the reader of the engine asked whether a total per family is wanted as well. I did not add one.

BHW coefficient reduction is named for Stage 1c in A8 but is a row rule next to tightening, not a column rule, and is not part of this design. Its check (the same 0/1 feasible set by enumeration for at most 12 columns) would go into the structure check as a fifth reader. Decide whether it is built with milestone 5 or after the gate.
